passage: I'm Madhuri's younger brother, and I've shared a flat with her and Jeevan since June. I've watched the same loop maybe ten times. Something small goes wrong, like Jeevan forgetting to call from a work trip. Madhuri asks what's wrong, then asks again, louder. Jeevan says "Nothing," and goes to the balcony. She follows. He puts his earphones in. She cries; he goes for a drive. Last Sunday something changed. Madhuri drew two arrows on the fridge whiteboard, one chasing, one running, making a circle. "This is us," she said. "Not you, not me. Us." Jeevan actually laughed. Then he stayed at the table. I don't know what they were feeling inside, but they talked for an hour.

qa.q: What did Madhuri draw on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: She drew two arrows, one chasing and one running, making a circle.

qa.q: What might Madhuri be feeling when she asks again, louder?
qa.a: She may feel anxious and shut out, needing reassurance that nothing is wrong between them.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Sunday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Madhuri showed the loop as "us", not one person's fault, which let Jeevan relax and stay to talk.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the whiteboard drawing?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to be blamed, which is why he laughs and stays at the table.

grounding: A brother watches a couple's pursue-and-withdraw loop and sees it ease once they treat it as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

passage:
Diwali weekend: At the family lunch, Chetan watched his cousin Irawati and her husband Deven. Irawati kept asking why Deven was so quiet; the more she asked, the further he retreated, until he was on the terrace with the kids.
Two weeks later: Chetan had them over for dinner and saw it again, only faster. Afterwards Irawati cried in his kitchen. "Why does he always run?" Chetan said carefully, "Maybe you both have a part. You chase when he goes quiet, he goes quiet when you chase. Like a see-saw."
New Year's Eve: At the party, when Deven went quiet, Irawati said lightly, "See-saw moment?" Deven smiled. "Yes. Give me ten minutes, then I'm back." He came back in ten.

qa.q: Where did Deven retreat to at the Diwali lunch?
qa.a: He retreated to the terrace with the kids.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she cried in Chetan's kitchen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and frustrated, believing Deven always runs from her.

qa.q: What turning point did Chetan offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: He described the pattern as a see-saw they both take part in, which let them spot it together instead of blaming one person.

qa.q: How might Deven feel when Irawati says "See-saw moment?" lightly?
qa.a: He probably feels understood rather than chased, so he can say what he needs and come back.

grounding: Over several weeks, a cousin watches a pursue-and-withdraw loop and helps the couple see it as a shared pattern, which opens a way out.

passage: When I was twenty-five, beta, I lived with my brother Uday and his new wife, Kamini, in a tiny Delhi flat. I watched them every evening like a play. Kamini would ask, "Why so quiet?" Uday would say, "Nothing," and pick up the paper. She'd ask again, louder. He'd go for a walk. She'd cry. He'd stay out longer. Each made the other worse, and each told me the other was the problem. One night I, Alka, the nosy sister, drew it on the back of an envelope: arrows going round and round. "It's not you, and it's not you," I said. "It's this circle." They laughed, then went very quiet. Kamini started asking once; Uday started coming back in ten minutes. That drawing stayed on their fridge for years.

qa.q: What did Alka draw on the back of the envelope?
qa.a: Arrows going round and round.

qa.q: What was young Alka feeling as she watched them every evening?
qa.a: She was worried and frustrated, seeing both of them hurting and blaming each other.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Alka's drawing showed the loop as a shared circle, so each could change their own part.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt when Kamini asked again, louder?
qa.a: Uday likely felt pressured and overwhelmed, so he withdrew on a walk, which made Kamini more upset.

grounding: Shows an observer who sees a pursue-withdraw loop and helps the couple see it as a shared pattern, not one person's fault.

passage: The tyre burst forty kilometres from Nainital, in the rain, and Ramesh stood by the car with his friends Usha and Deven while the driver changed it. Within ten minutes they were at it again. Usha: "You didn't check the tyres, did you? You never tell me anything." Deven turned away and stared at the valley. Usha followed him, voice rising. Deven walked further. Ramesh, holding the umbrella, had seen this loop all trip, at breakfast, at the hotel desk. Later, in the dhaba, he said carefully, "Can I say something? When Usha pushes, Deven pulls away, and then Usha pushes harder. You're both stuck on the same wheel." They looked at each other. Deven said, "I do go quiet." Usha said, "And I chase." The rest of the drive felt lighter.

qa.q: Where were they when the tyre burst?
qa.a: Forty kilometres from Nainital, in the rain.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he watched the loop repeat all trip?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and concerned, careful about how to say what he had seen.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh's words help?
qa.a: He described the pattern as a shared wheel, so neither Usha nor Deven had to be the one at fault.

qa.q: How might Deven feel when Usha follows him with a rising voice?
qa.a: Deven probably feels cornered and overwhelmed, so he walks further away.

grounding: Illustrates an observer naming a pursue-withdraw loop between two partners as a shared pattern, which eases the conflict.

passage: From the sofa in their shared Pune flat, Vasudha could hear it through the wall again: Dilnaz on the phone to Joel, "Why didn't you call at lunch?", then a long pause, then "Say something!" Then the call ending, Dilnaz crying, and twenty minutes later another call. Vasudha knew Joel from college. He wasn't cruel, just the kind who went still when things got loud. And the stiller he got, the louder Dilnaz got. On Sunday, over poha, Vasudha said, "I don't think either of you is the villain. It's like a see-saw: you push, he freezes, you push harder." Dilnaz put her spoon down. "So it's my fault?" "No. It's the see-saw. You could both step off." That night Dilnaz texted Joel: "Can we talk about the pattern, not about who's wrong?"

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Dilnaz eat on Sunday?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she listened through the wall?
qa.a: She felt worried for Dilnaz and sad, seeing the calls go round in circles.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do well when she spoke to Dilnaz?
qa.a: She described a shared see-saw instead of blaming one person, which let Dilnaz reframe the problem.

qa.q: How might Joel react to Dilnaz's text about the pattern?
qa.a: Joel may feel relieved and less attacked, since the message is about the pattern, not about who is wrong.

grounding: Shows an observer helping a friend see an anxious-avoidant loop as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

Aditi had been staying with her sister Binita for two days when it happened again.
"You're checking your phone. Are you upset with me?" Binita asked.
"No," said Vikram, standing up. "I'm going to the balcony."
"See, you're leaving!"
"I'm leaving because you're following me!"
Later, Aditi found Binita in the kitchen. "Can I say what I'm seeing, Bini?"
"That he's cold?"
"That you chase when you're scared, and he hides when he's crowded. Then you chase harder, and he hides further. It's a circle. Nobody's the villain."
Binita was quiet. "It feels like his fault."
"I know. Maybe you could both look at the circle together? Even with a couples counsellor?"
That night, Aditi heard them on the balcony, talking quietly, for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where did Vikram go when Binita asked if he was upset?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel watching the argument, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: She was worried and wanted to help, so she gently asked Binita whether she could say what she was seeing.

qa.q: Why could seeing the pattern as a circle help Binita and Vikram?
qa.a: It stops them blaming one person and lets them notice together how chasing and hiding feed each other, which opens a way out.

qa.q: How might Vikram experience Binita's questions?
qa.a: Vikram seems to feel crowded when Binita follows him, so he pulls away to the balcony, even if he is not upset with her.

grounding: Shows a sister observing a couple's pursue-and-withdraw loop and naming it as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.
